content.title: Data Distribution, Outliers, and Measures of Center and Spread
content.overview: This lesson focuses on analyzing the distribution shapes of one-variable data, identifying outliers, and understanding how these factors influence measures of center (mean, median) and measures of spread (standard deviation, range).
learning_objectives: Identify symmetric, left-skewed, and right-skewed distributions.
Understand the different impacts of outliers on the mean and median.
Analyze the relationship between distribution shape and the relative values of the mean and median.
Evaluate the impact of outliers on measures of spread such as standard deviation and range.

sections.title: Shapes of Data Distributions
sections.content: Data distributions generally fall into three main shapes: 1. Symmetric: Data is evenly distributed on both sides of the center; the mean is typically equal to the median. 2. Right-skewed (Positively skewed): The tail extends to the right, containing a few very large values. In this distribution, the mean is typically greater than the median. 3. Left-skewed (Negatively skewed): The tail extends to the left, containing a few very small values. In this distribution, the mean is typically less than the median.

sections.title: Outliers and Their Effects
sections.content:
An outlier is an observation that is significantly different from the other values in a data set. Outliers affect statistics to varying degrees: The mean is highly sensitive to outliers and is pulled in the direction of the outlier. The median is robust, meaning it is less affected by outliers. When extreme outliers are present, the median is often a better indicator of a 'typical' value.

![Impact of Outliers on Statistics](https://img.justsolvely.com/followUpImage/087c2343-8318-4da2-afee-77377cf7b66a-1786502065860-75.webp)

sections.title: Measures of Spread: Standard Deviation and Range
sections.content: Spread describes the variability of data. Standard deviation measures the average distance of data points from the mean. The more spread out the data, the larger the standard deviation. Range is the difference between the maximum and minimum values. The presence of outliers significantly increases the range and usually increases the standard deviation because it increases the distance between data points and the mean.

worked_examples.question: A data set containing 5 numbers is {10, 12, 14, 15, 100}. If the outlier 100 is removed, how will the mean and median change?
worked_examples.solution: 1. Calculate original data: Mean = (10+12+14+15+100)/5 = 30.2; Median = 14. 2. After removing 100: The data set is {10, 12, 14, 15}. New Mean = (10+12+14+15)/4 = 12.75; New Median = (12+14)/2 = 13. 3. Conclusion: The mean decreased significantly from 30.2 to 12.75, while the median only decreased slightly from 14 to 13. This demonstrates that the mean is more affected by outliers.

common_mistakes: Incorrectly believing that the median is always heavily influenced by outliers.
Confusing left-skewed and right-skewed: remember that 'skew' refers to the direction of the tail, not where the data is most dense.
Thinking standard deviation only depends on the size of the values, ignoring that it depends on the spread of data relative to the mean.
exam_tips: On the SAT, if a question asks which statistic is least affected by an outlier, the answer is usually the 'median'.
If a distribution graph shows a long tail on the right, the mean must be greater than the median.
When comparing the standard deviation of two distributions, look at which graph has data more 'clustered' around the center; the more clustered distribution has a smaller standard deviation.
content.recap: Understanding distribution shapes (symmetric, left-skewed, right-skewed) is key to predicting the relationship between the mean and median. Outliers significantly pull the mean and increase the standard deviation, but have a limited effect on the median.

knowledge_claims.content: A right-skewed distribution is a shape where the tail of the data extends toward the larger values on the right side.
In a right-skewed distribution, the mean is typically greater than the median.
In a left-skewed distribution, the mean is typically less than the median.
In a perfectly symmetric distribution, the mean and median are typically equal.
The mean is highly sensitive to outliers and will be pulled in the direction of extreme values.
The median is robust against outliers, meaning it is affected much less by extreme values than the mean is.
Standard deviation measures the average spread of data points relative to the mean.
Adding an outlier that is far from the mean typically increases the standard deviation of a data set.
The range is the difference between the maximum and minimum values in a data set and is highly susceptible to outliers.
Standard deviation cannot be judged solely by the height of a graph; one must observe the horizontal width of the data distribution.
